statement: Diné (Navajo) arrival in the Southwest is genuinely contested and should be reported as a range with named methods, not a single date. Linguistic/glottochronological estimates (Harry Hoijer, 1956; Dell Hymes, 1957, building on Edward Sapir's 1915 Proto-Athabaskan phonology) place divergence of Proto-Apachean from Northern Athabaskan at roughly 1000-1300 years BP, with internal Apachean divergence roughly 400-600 years BP — glottochronology as a method is itself contested within historical linguistics generally. Archaeological consensus (Ronald H. Towner, Defending Dinétah: Pueblitos in the Ancestral Navajo Homeland, University of Utah Press, 2003, based on dendrochronological survey) finds no confidently-dated Apachean evidence in the Southwest predating c. 1500-1525, with the earliest Dinétah-phase forked-stick hogans clustering mid-16th century, though some tree-ring samples project occupation back to c. 1450. The harder archaeological/dendrochronological evidence clusters c. 1450-1525; linguistic dating is compatible but less precise and methodologically disputed.
scholarly_disagreement: Linguistic/glottochronological estimates (Hoijer 1956; Hymes 1957) suggest an earlier divergence window (roughly 1000-1300 years BP for Proto-Apachean) than the archaeological/dendrochronological floor (Towner 2003), which finds no confidently-dated Navajo presence in the Southwest earlier than c. 1450-1525; the two methods are not fully reconciled.

sources.citation: Towner, Ronald H. Defending Dinétah: Pueblitos in the Ancestral Navajo Homeland. Salt Lake City: University of Utah Press, 2003.
sources.author: Ronald H. Towner

interpretations.position: Proto-Apachean diverged from Northern Athabaskan roughly 1000-1300 years BP, implying an earlier Southwest arrival window than the archaeological record alone supports
interpretations.strongest_case: Builds on Edward Sapir's 1915 Proto-Athabaskan phonological reconstruction to estimate a divergence date independent of archaeological preservation bias.

interpretations.position: No confidently-dated Apachean archaeological evidence in the Southwest predates c. 1450-1525; earlier dates are not empirically supported

interpretations.strongest_case: Tree-ring-dated forked-stick hogans provide a direct, checkable material floor, unlike glottochronology's contested rate assumptions.
